title: Decidability, complexity and the compiler link
subtitle: Some questions no program can answer; others can be answered, but not quickly. And why every compiler is a pair of these machines.

sections.title: The Church–Turing thesis and universal machines
sections.body: The Church–Turing thesis: anything computable by an algorithm is computable by a Turing machine. It cannot be proved (“algorithm” is informal) but every model ever proposed agrees. A universal Turing machine takes the encoding of any machine M and an input w on its tape and simulates M on w — the idea of the stored-program computer.

questions.prompt: A universal Turing machine corresponds to…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Programs are just data on the tape.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — the universal machine
figures.note: One machine that runs all machines.

sections.title: The halting problem
sections.body: Is there a program H(P, x) that always correctly says whether program P halts on input x? No. Suppose H existed and build D(P): run H(P, P); if H says “halts”, loop forever; otherwise halt. Now ask about D(D): if H(D, D) says it halts then D loops; if it says it loops then D halts. Either way H is wrong — a contradiction, by diagonalisation. So the halting problem is undecidable, and by reduction so are many others (does this program ever print “hello”? do two programs compute the same function?).

questions.prompt: What does the halting problem show?

choices.text: No algorithm can decide, for every program and input, whether it halts.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Some well-defined questions are beyond any computer.

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — why no halting decider exists
figures.note: The self-referential trick behind the proof.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
[Assume H(P, x) decides halting] as h #blue
[Build D(P): if H(P, P) says halts → loop; else → halt] as d #amber
<What does D(D) do?> as q #violet
[If it halts, H said “halts”, so D loops] as a #rose
[If it loops, H said “loops”, so D halts] as b #rose
(Contradiction: H cannot exist) as c
h -> d
d -> q
q -> a : halts?
q -> b : loops?
a -> c
b -> c");

sections.title: Time complexity: P and NP
sections.body: P is the set of problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic machine (sorting, shortest path). NP is the set whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time (equivalently solved in polynomial time by a nondeterministic machine): factoring, Hamiltonian cycle, SAT. Clearly P ⊆ NP; whether P = NP is the most famous open problem. A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time: solve one fast and you solve them all.

worked.why: Verifying a proposed Hamiltonian cycle in a graph of n vertices means checking each consecutive pair is an edge and every vertex appears once.
That is O(n) — polynomial — so the problem is in NP. Finding one by trying all orders takes up to n! steps.

questions.prompt: What is special about NP-complete problems?

choices.text: Every problem in NP reduces to them; a fast algorithm for one would give one for all.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: They are solvable, just apparently slow.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: They are the hardest problems in NP.

sections.title: The compiler link: lexical analysis = DFA
sections.body: A compiler’s first phase, the lexical analyser, turns characters into tokens (identifiers, numbers, keywords). Each token class is a regular expression; the scanner is a DFA built from them. Here a tiny DFA recognises identifiers: a letter then letters or digits.

questions.prompt: Which automaton underlies a lexical analyser?

choices.text: A DFA built from the token regular expressions.

sections.title: Syntax analysis = CFG and PDA
sections.body: The parser checks that the token stream fits the language’s context-free grammar and builds a parse tree. Top-down (recursive descent, LL) expands from the start symbol; bottom-up (shift–reduce, LR) reduces the input back to the start symbol using a stack — a PDA. Nested brackets and blocks need the stack, which is why a regular expression alone cannot parse a program.

worked.why: Stack-based check of (a+a)*a: shift (, a, reduce a→F→T→E, shift +, a, reduce, reduce E+T→E, shift ), reduce (E)→F, and so on.
Finally reduce T*F → T → E: the whole input is the start symbol.

questions.prompt: Bottom-up parsing uses a stack to…

choices.text: Hold symbols waiting to be reduced by a grammar rule.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Shift pushes a token; reduce replaces a rule’s right-hand side by its variable.

figures.caption: Figure 6.2.1 — parsing (a+a)*a
figures.note: The parse tree of an expression with brackets.
figures.script: var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"pt","engine":"cfg","grammar":"E -> E+T | T\nT -> T*F | F\nF -> (E) | a","string":"(a+a)*a","width":600,"height":440});

problems.prompt: Why is a parser built on a context-free grammar rather than a regular expression?
problems.answer: Programs have arbitrarily nested constructs — brackets, blocks, function calls — and matching them needs unbounded memory (a stack). Regular languages cannot do that (the pumping lemma argument for aⁿbⁿ), context-free ones can.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Halting is undecidable; some problems are solvable but not efficiently (NP-complete).
  • Compilers: lexer = DFA, parser = PDA/CFG.
